nameStory: The smoothish-stemmed bolete gets its name from its relatively smooth stem surface, which helps distinguish it from many other boletes that have rougher, more textured stems. The scientific name 'subglabripes' literally means 'somewhat smooth-footed,' referring to this key identifying feature that early mycologists like Charles Horton Peck noticed when he first described it in 1887.
description: The smoothish-stemmed bolete is a medium-sized mushroom with the classic bolete look - a brownish cap sitting atop a yellowish stem with tiny pores instead of gills underneath. The cap ranges from about 3-4 inches across, while the stem stands 2-4 inches tall and feels relatively smooth to the touch. Like other boletes, it has a sturdy, substantial feel and produces an olive-brown spore print. The flesh inside is typically yellow and may show a light blue color change when cut or bruised.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Yellowish stem that feels notably smooth or only slightly textured when you run your finger along it, quite different from the rough, scaly stems of many other boletes

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Brownish cap that's 3-4 inches wide with a dry, matte surface that doesn't feel slimy or sticky even when moist

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Tiny pore surface underneath the cap instead of gills, typical of all bolete mushrooms, starting yellowish and aging to olive tones

idTips.label: Bruising
idTips.description: Yellow flesh that may slowly turn light blue when cut or damaged, though this color change is often subtle and not always present

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, pleasant mushroom smell with no strong or unpleasant odors - nothing sour, fishy, or chemical

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Olive-brown spore print when cap is placed gill-side down on white paper overnight

habitat: Look for smoothish-stemmed boletes in mixed hardwood forests throughout New England, particularly near oak, maple, and beech trees. They form beneficial partnerships (mycorrhizal relationships) with these tree roots, so you'll find them growing from the soil rather than on decaying wood. They prefer well-drained forest floors with rich leaf litter.

seasonality.spring: Not typically found in spring as this species fruits later in the growing season.
seasonality.summer: Prime season begins in July with young, firm specimens appearing after warm rains in hardwood areas.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting through August and September, though specimens become softer and may be past prime for identification or collection.
seasonality.winter: Not found in winter as this species cannot tolerate freezing temperatures.

funFact: This bolete was actually discovered and named right here in New England by Charles Horton Peck, a legendary mycologist who described over 2,700 species of fungi, many from his base in Albany, New York - making this a true regional native with local scientific heritage!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other yellowish-stemmed boletes, but the relatively smooth stem texture is your best clue. Many similar boletes have obviously rough, scaly, or dotted stems, so take time to really feel the stem surface - if it's notably smoother than expected, you might have found a smoothish-stemmed bolete.
contextualKnowledge: This mushroom was shuffled between different scientific groups based on DNA studies in 2015, moving from the old Boletus genus to the newer Hemileccinum genus. This reflects how modern genetic tools are helping scientists understand the true relationships between different bolete species.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives in the Hemileccinum genus, the smoothish-stemmed bolete is the most commonly encountered in New England. The ashtray bolete has a distinctive unpleasant smell and more obvious red dotting on the stem, while the corrugated bolete has much more textured, wrinkled cap and stem surfaces. The smooth stem really sets this species apart from both of its regional cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relatives in the Hemileccinum genus, the Ashtray Bolete is distinguished primarily by its smoky odor and the red dotting on its stem.
